Stellifer brasiliensis is a small-bodied sciaenid that inhabits the shallow coastal waters of Brazil, where it completes its entire life cycle under warm, stable thermal conditions. Females of this species reach a maximum recorded total length of 22.2 cm [Li = 22.2 cm], representing the largest size documented in wild-caught individuals. The onset of sexual maturity occurs at a considerably smaller body size, with puberty triggered at a total length of 7.3 cm [Lp = 7.3 cm], a threshold that aligns with the pattern observed in other short-lived sciaenids that prioritize early maturation over prolonged somatic growth. At birth, newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are extraordinarily small, with a wet weight at birth of 0.00053 grams [Wwb = 0.00053 grams]. This diminutive starting mass imposes a period of intense vulnerability during the planktonic larval phase, during which rapid growth is critical for transitioning to exogenous feeding and avoiding predation.

Reproductive output in the Brazilian stardrum has been characterized through histological examination of ovarian tissue from gravid females collected during the peak spawning season. At the prevailing water temperature of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C], females produce approximately 69 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 69 eggs per spawning event], with a spawning frequency of roughly one event per day [F_R_i = roughly one event per day] throughout the protracted breeding period. This high-frequency, low-fecundity reproductive strategy is typical of tropical sciaenids that inhabit warm, productive waters where larval food sources are abundant but predation pressure on eggs is extreme. The total daily reproductive output implied by this combination of batch fecundity and spawning interval results in a remarkably high annual fecundity, enabling the species to offset the elevated mortality rates that characterize the early pelagic egg and yolk-sac larval stages.

The ultimate wet weight achieved by mature individuals of Stellifer brasiliensis has been estimated at 126 grams [Wwi = 126 grams], a value derived from the length-weight relationship established for this species in southeastern Brazilian waters. This asymptotic mass is attained only by the largest and oldest females in the population, corresponding to individuals that have achieved the maximum total length of 22.2 cm [Li = 22.2 cm]. By contrast, females that have just reached the size threshold for puberty at 7.3 cm [Lp = 7.3 cm] exhibit a markedly lower body mass, with the wet weight at puberty for females calculated to be 4 grams [Wwp = 4 grams]. This nearly thirty-fold increase in body mass from puberty to the ultimate size illustrates the substantial investment in somatic growth that occurs after the onset of reproductive maturity, a pattern that is uncommon among small-bodied fishes.

Longevity data for Stellifer brasiliensis indicate that this species has a relatively compressed life history, with field-based mark-recapture studies conducted at a stable water temperature of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C] documenting a maximum lifespan of 11 years [am = 11 years]. This lifespan is somewhat longer than that reported for many congeners of similar body size, likely reflecting the relatively stable thermal regime and consistent food availability in the coastal nursery habitats it occupies. The warm water is permissive for sustained growth and high metabolic activity, allowing individuals to channel energy into both reproduction and continued somatic increase throughout much of their adult lives. In the context of the extreme female mass gain from 4 grams [Wwp = 4 grams] at puberty to 126 grams [Wwi = 126 grams] at ultimate size, the observed longevity highlights a strategy of extended iteroparity.

Comparative analysis within the Sciaenidae reveals that the Brazilian stardrum occupies an intermediate position on the life-history continuum between short-lived, single-season spawners and longer-lived offshore species. The total length at puberty of 7.3 cm [Lp = 7.3 cm] is proportionally early relative to the ultimate length of 22.2 cm [Li = 22.2 cm], representing a maturation size of roughly 33 percent of maximum length, which is a common threshold among warm-water sciaenids that face high adult mortality. Interestingly, the wet weight at birth of 0.00053 grams [Wwb = 0.00053 grams] is remarkably consistent across the family, reflecting the conserved spherical egg morphology that yields a predictable hatchling mass from a 1 millimeter diameter fertilized ovum. Under the stable thermal regime of 23.9 °C [T = 23.9 °C], the combination of a long 11 years [am = 11 years] lifespan and the high daily reproductive rate sustains population resilience despite intense larval mortality, a dynamic that is central to the species' ecological success in dynamic coastal ecosystems.
